luganda: Omuwana wa mwanyoko oba mugandawo - omujjwa (nga omulenzi)

english: To be in pain / To hurt
I go to work every day.
I work in the agriculture department.

luganda: Ku makya tunywa chai ne mutabani wange.
english: In the morning we drink tea with my son.
My son goes to school every day.
I have a bag with a file of papers.

luganda: Bwe nva eka ntambula ate ne ninya takisi.
english: From home I walk then I take a taxi.

luganda: Nkola okutuuka ku ssaawa kumi n'emu ez'olweggulo era nenzigalawo offeesi.
english: I work up to five in the evening then I close the office.
Today she is going to hospital.
The elder child, Jane, is sick.
She is now brushing her teeth.

luganda: Omwana omuto Musa akuba engatto eddagala.
english: The young one, Moses, is polishing his shoes.
It is late, she is eating while standing.

luganda: Kakati atunula mu ddirisa alabe oba waliyo mmotoka ejja.
english: She is now looking out of the window to see if there is any vehicle coming.

luganda: Omwana omuto akaaba kubanga maama ne Jane bagenda.
english: The child was crying because mother and Jane were going.

luganda: Baabo basitula ensawo era bafuluma mu nnyumba.
english: There they are now carrying the bag and going out of the house.
One was a man and the other was a woman.

luganda: Omusajja yali mupunta nga ate mukyala we mubazi w'abitabo.
english: The man was an architect while his wife was an accountant.

luganda: Omwami ye yafumba ate omukyala n'asiika enva.
english: The man cooked while the woman fried the sauce.
The woman washed the clothes while the man dried them.
When the woman was angry, the man made her laugh.

luganda: Omwami yalongoosa eddiiro omukyala nayera ekisenge.
english: The man cleaned the sitting room, the woman swept the bedroom.

luganda: Omwami bwe yasaawa olugya omukyala nayera emanju.
english: The man slashed the compound and the woman swept the backyard.

luganda: Olumu omukyala yali adduka embwa nagwa wansi.
english: One time the woman fell down while running from a dog.

luganda: Omwami yabuuka n'atomera omwango gwoluggi nagwa wansi.
english: The man jumped, knocked the door frame and fell.

luganda: Bombi ne bakaaba. Buli omu yakwata omukono gwa munne ne bagenda mu ddwaliro.
english: Both cried. Each one held the other's hand and both went to hospital.
I am going to the shops.
What amount? What is the price?
Leave this one, I do not want it.
It is too large / too much.
It is too small / too little.
What do you have in the shop?
I have forgotten my baggage in the car.
I am late, the train has left without me.
I have missed the plane. What can I do?
Somebody is disturbing me, I will call the police!
I have been robbed. Who is in charge here?

luganda: Lino ekkubo ligenda wa? Liyitamu emmotoka?
english: Where does this road lead? Is it motorable?

luganda: Kino ekifo bakiyita batya? Ate ekibuga ekiddako?
english: What is this place called? What is the next town?
Can I leave the car here briefly?

luganda: Mulina omukka? Kebera amafuta, woyilo, n'amazzi.
english: Do you have tyre pressure? Check petrol, oil, and water.

luganda: Lajenta mulimu amazzi? Kebera omukka gw'emipiira.
english: Is there water in the radiator? Check the tyre pressure.
My car is stuck in the mud.
The valve is spoilt and the bonnet is bent.
We are happy to see you.
I am happy too. / Me too.
Thank you for all you are doing.
How is the rest of the family?

luganda: Gyetuli bulungi nnyabo. Tukola tubeewo, n'abeeka balungi.
english: We are okay, Madam. We work just for a living, and at home people are fine.
It has been a long time since we last saw you.

luganda: Naffe; anti olaba ensi etumazeeko ekiseera okulabagana ate n'emitawaana mingi.
english: Even us — the world is so busy that we cannot spare time to see each other.
Congratulations on building. It is a big house.
Please help me and tell me.
Excuse me — do you understand English?
Have pity on me, it is very bad.

luganda: Nsaaliddwa, ndi mu bwangu era noonya.
english: I am disappointed, I am in a hurry, and I am still searching.
I think there is cold and warmth today.
It is my fault. I do not know if it is true.
Wait a moment, here is the direction.
Which way will you pass through?
Will you pass by the market?
Which route will you return by?
Try it. / Give it a go.
Come back another time. / You are always welcome.

notes: [hardwork] Whatever you plant without care, or whatever you invest effort into, that is what you will benefit from. Your outcomes depend on your own actions.

english: One by one makes a bundle.
notes: [hardwork] Small, consistent efforts accumulate into something great. Never underestimate a small beginning.

english: One who seeks a better life does not put down the hand.
notes: [hardwork] If you truly want to improve your life, you must never stop working. Persistence is essential.
[hardwork] To achieve anything in life, you must work tirelessly without stopping, just as a person under pressure cannot rest until the work is done.

luganda: Akwata empola atuuka wala, nawolovu atuuka emitala
english: One who moves slowly but surely reaches far; the chameleon reaches very far.
notes: [hardwork] Patience and steady effort lead to greater success than rushing. Taking things carefully is always better than haste.

english: The bone that was not stolen is thrown freely at the front of the house.
notes: [hardwork] Work for what you have so that you can be free in society. Only what you earned honestly can you enjoy openly.

english: If you wait for the end, you will only pierce the tail.
notes: [hardwork] Do not procrastinate. Act when the opportunity is right, not after it has passed. Waiting too long means you miss the chance.
[hardwork] When people work together, they achieve more. Unity and teamwork produce the best results.

english: A woman who bears children is better than one who always slaughters a cow.
notes: [hardwork] Something that gives lasting, living value is better than temporary material wealth. Family and long-term investment matter more than short-term gains.

english: A foolish person should not make you foolish.
notes: [wisdom] Never let someone else's poor judgment drag you down. Stay wise even when surrounded by foolishness.

luganda: Nditwaala kinene afa tatuuse ku buko
english: One waiting to get something big dies before the introduction.
notes: [wisdom] It is better to go with the little you have than to wait for something bigger that may never come. Seize current opportunities.

english: Friendship is like hot fat — enjoy it while it is still warm.
notes: [wisdom] Relationships and love are sweet at their best moments. Cherish them while they last because they can cool and change.

luganda: Ababiri babibira ebigambo naye abasatu babisatulula
english: Two people keep secrets but three people destroy them.
notes: [wisdom] The more people know a secret, the harder it is to keep. Be careful who you share private matters with.

luganda: Gwotazinanga naye bwasituka okuzina nga gwe otuula
english: One you have never danced with — when they start dancing, it is as if you are seated.
notes: [wisdom] Someone you have not worked or partnered with can overtake you when they start. Do not underestimate newcomers.

english: Rich people love each other (they stay together).
notes: [wisdom] People of the same level or class tend to associate together. Wealth attracts wealth.

luganda: Amaka abiri musango, bwolwanira agali e kyaggwe nga ge ssingo banyaga
english: Two families are a fight — when you fight for the one in Kyaggwe, the one in Ssingo is taken.
notes: [wisdom] Managing two households or divided loyalties always leads to trouble. Polygamy and divided attention create endless conflict.

luganda: Bakuseeredde mu katale oyombera mu kubo
english: You were ripped off in the market but you are arguing about it in the road.
notes: [wisdom] Solve problems where they happen, not later and elsewhere. Complaining after the moment has passed accomplishes nothing.

english: A small thing that is available is worth more than a big thing that has only been promised.
notes: [wisdom] Something real and available — even if small — is better than a grand promise that may never be fulfilled.
[wisdom] Relationships need constant effort, creativity, and new energy to survive. Love that is not nurtured will die.
[wisdom] Be careful with visitors — when they leave, they will talk about what they saw in your home. Maintain your standards always.

english: One who loses the only thing they have in life stays miserable forever.
notes: [wisdom] When someone loses their only source of hope or support, their suffering never ends. Guard what you love most.

english: One who has not walked your journey will tell you it is like peeling a banana.
notes: [wisdom] Someone who has never been through what you have experienced will always make it sound easy. Do not take advice from those with no experience.

luganda: Abasajja kiti kya muwogo wokisuula wekilandira
english: Men are like stems of a cassava plant — wherever you dump them, they grow.
notes: [wisdom] Men adapt and move on easily. When rejected or left, they simply start again somewhere else.

english: A shoot of a musa banana turns into beer.
notes: [wisdom] Something that looks small and insignificant today can become something great and valuable in the future. Never write off potential.

luganda: Ssekibojera ku lwazi kyeyesigga mumwa mugumu
english: The bird that pecks at a rock is sure of its strong beak.
notes: [wisdom] Attempt only what you know you are capable of. Confidence in action comes from knowing your own strength.

english: Over-praising a man can lead him to be eaten by a leopard.
notes: [wisdom] Too much flattery makes a person overconfident and reckless. Excessive praise can lead someone into dangerous mistakes.

english: One can claim to have many friends until they fall on hard times.
notes: [wisdom] You do not know who your true friends are until you face difficulty. Hard times reveal the truth about relationships.

english: When money is lost, one stays home.
notes: [wisdom] A person who loses money becomes lazy and stays home complaining instead of going out to earn more.

english: A small healthy thing is better than a big unhealthy one.
notes: [wisdom] Quality matters more than size or quantity. A small thing that works well is more valuable than a big thing that does not.

luganda: Okwambala obulungyi ssi kuwasa, ssinga ekajjo lyenjovu lyawangiza muzibu gwazaalampanga
english: Dressing well is not the same as marrying well; do not judge by appearance.
notes: [wisdom] Appearances can be deceiving. Beautiful clothes or looks do not tell you about a person's character or suitability as a partner.

english: A woman who farms with her husband is not weak.
notes: [wisdom] A hardworking woman who partners with her husband in all things shows strength, not weakness.

english: One who wrongs you makes you forget God.
notes: [wisdom] When someone deeply wrongs you, the anger can make you forget your values and want to retaliate. Be careful not to let others drag you away from your principles.

english: One who accepts their mistake pays little.
notes: [wisdom] Accepting and admitting a mistake costs you less than denying it. Honesty in error reduces consequences.

luganda: Kaggwe ensonyi nga omukazi ayomba ne bba
english: Shamelessness is when a woman quarrels with her husband in public.
notes: [respect] A woman who publicly quarrels with her husband shows a lack of humility and respect for the home. This proverb reflects traditional Baganda social expectations.

english: The head of the house must be respected.
notes: [respect] The leader of a home or a workplace deserves respect and should be honored by those under them.

english: A visitor should not act like they own the house.
notes: [respect] Guests should respect the rules and customs of the home they visit. Do not overstep your boundaries as a visitor.

luganda: Ofunda nomubi ngazaala ngalima nga ayanilriza naabagenyi
english: It is better to be with an ugly one who bears children, farms and is hospitable.
notes: [respect] Character and contribution matter far more than beauty. A hardworking and hospitable partner is more valuable than an attractive but unproductive one.

english: The banana plant fades the way you look after it.
notes: [respect] How you treat what you own determines how it thrives. A person — especially in marriage — will fade if not cared for and respected.

luganda: Akaggo akaakuba muka balo bwokalaba okasuka mu muliro
english: A stick that was used to beat your co-wife — when you see it, throw it in the fire.
notes: [respect] Get rid of things that caused harm or trouble in the past. Learn from others' painful experiences and do not repeat the same mistakes.

english: What burns the poor also burns the rich.
notes: [respect] No one is exempt from consequences or suffering. Wealth and status do not protect you from the same challenges that affect everyone.

english: Secrets of the house should stay inside the house.
notes: [respect] Family matters should be handled privately. Do not expose household problems to outsiders. What happens at home stays at home.

english: The usefulness of a calabash is predicted by its handle.
notes: [respect] You can predict a person's future usefulness by their early behaviour. First impressions and early character reveal much about the future.

english: The disease that catches the husband does not spare the wife.
notes: [respect] Partners share consequences. What affects one in a marriage affects the other. Be faithful and honest because your actions impact your spouse.

english: An ungrateful person has no one to give them anything.
notes: [respect] Gratitude is essential. People who do not appreciate what they receive eventually find no one willing to help them.

english: One you trained can chase you away.
notes: [respect] Someone you taught and raised up can eventually surpass and reject you. Do not underestimate those you mentor.

luganda: Ekiddiba kidda wabwe wakyo, essaaniiko lidda much lusukku
english: Leftovers get back to their owners; banana leaves return to the plantation.
notes: [respect] Everything finds its way back to where it belongs. People who leave always come home. Justice also returns to its source.

english: An elder's eye sees even in a dirty place.
notes: [respect] Elders have experience and wisdom that allows them to see things others miss. They should be respected and their guidance heeded.

luganda: Munno mu kabi, ye munno ddala
english: Your friend in trouble is your true friend.
notes: [wisdom] Genuine friendship is revealed in hardship. Those who stand by you when things are difficult are your real allies.

english: Go round the long way and arrive in safety.
notes: [wisdom] It is wiser to take a longer, safer path than to rush through a dangerous shortcut. Safety is worth the extra effort.

english: People who live together cannot fail to have quarrels.
notes: [wisdom] Conflict is natural in any close relationship. Do not be surprised when people who share space disagree — it is normal.

english: Relations are like beer-calabashes; they bump against each other but do not break.
notes: [wisdom] Family members will always have disagreements and conflicts, but the bonds of family are strong enough to survive them.

english: Brandishing weapons does not affect the legs, but the mouth.
notes: [wisdom] The harm from boasting and threatening words falls back on the speaker. Boastful talk causes more harm to the one speaking than to the target.

luganda: Ebukojja banjagala nga nyoko akyali mulamu
english: Your mother's relatives only love you whilst she is still alive.
notes: [wisdom] Some relationships exist only because of a connecting person. When that person is gone, the bonds may dissolve. Value relationships built on genuine love.

english: He who is not in love himself says they are infatuated.
notes: [wisdom] People who have not experienced something tend to judge it harshly. Do not criticize what you have not lived.

luganda: Okwagalana kyayi kya mpiso, bwe kitasoba tikitunga
english: Mutual love is like thread in a needle — if it does not pass through and stick out, it does not sew.
notes: [wisdom] Love must flow in both directions to be effective. One-sided love cannot build or hold a relationship together.

english: Do not count what you have not yet got; they took back the bananas you had stolen at night.
notes: [wisdom] Do not assume you own something before it is secured. Premature counting of gains can lead to disappointment.

luganda: Abalungi mbwa ya nnamaaso, bw'etebba n'eyigga
english: The beautiful are like a dog with big eyes — might turn out to be a thief or a good hunter.
notes: [wisdom] Beauty tells you nothing about a person's true character. An attractive person may be harmful or helpful — you cannot know from looks alone.

english: He who takes you at night, you thank him in the morning.
notes: [wisdom] Sometimes the value of someone's help is only understood later. Be grateful even for those who helped you in dark or difficult times.

luganda: Luganda Consonants Are Similar to English
english: Luganda uses almost all the same consonants as English. The only two consonant letters from the English alphabet that are NOT used in standard Luganda are X and Q. All other consonants appear in Luganda words.
notes: Luganda uses almost all the same consonants as English. The only two consonant letters from the English alphabet that are NOT used in standard Luganda are X and Q. All other consonants appear in Luganda words.

luganda: Each Consonant Pairs Cleanly With Each Vowel
english: In Luganda, every consonant combines directly and predictably with each vowel to produce a clean syllable sound. Unlike English, there are no silent letters or irregular combinations. What you see is what you say.
notes: In Luganda, every consonant combines directly and predictably with each vowel to produce a clean syllable sound. Unlike English, there are no silent letters or irregular combinations. What you see is what you say.

luganda: Double Consonants Change Meaning — Always Write Them Correctly
english: In Luganda, writing a single consonant versus a double consonant (two of the same letter together) produces two completely different words. This is one of the most important spelling rules in Luganda. Getting it wrong does not just change the emphasis — it changes the entire meaning of the word.
notes: In Luganda, writing a single consonant versus a double consonant (two of the same letter together) produces two completely different words. This is one of the most important spelling rules in Luganda. Getting it wrong does not just change the emphasis — it changes the entire meaning of the word.

luganda: Common Two-Consonant Combinations That Function as One Sound
english: Luganda uses many two-consonant combinations that are read as a single blended sound. These must be learned as complete units. The most important ones are listed below with real word examples.
notes: Luganda uses many two-consonant combinations that are read as a single blended sound. These must be learned as complete units. The most important ones are listed below with real word examples.

english: Luganda has a special consonant sound that does not exist in English. It is the nasal velar sound — the 'ng' sound at the end of English words like 'sing' or 'king'. In Luganda, this sound can appear at the START of a word, which is unusual for English speakers. In modern Luganda writing it is written as 'ng'' (ng with an apostrophe) to distinguish it from a regular n+g combination.

luganda: The Letters R and L Sometimes Interchange
english: In Luganda, the letters R and L are related sounds and in some words they can be interchanged or appear as variants. Many Luganda speakers pronounce R and L similarly. You will find both spellings in different texts for the same word. This is a natural feature of the language.

english: Luganda, like English, has five vowels: A, E, I, O, U (both uppercase and lowercase). These vowels give sound and meaning to words. In Luganda, each vowel is read exactly as it sounds — it directly controls the pronunciation of the word.

english: In Luganda, the vowel in a word controls its pronunciation AND meaning. Unlike English where some vowels are silent or irregular, Luganda vowels are always pronounced as written and always affect meaning.
notes: In Luganda, the vowel in a word controls its pronunciation AND meaning. Unlike English where some vowels are silent or irregular, Luganda vowels are always pronounced as written and always affect meaning.

english: When two identical vowels appear together in a Luganda word (called a long vowel), they extend the sound AND change the meaning of the word entirely. This is a very important rule because using the wrong vowel length can produce a completely different word.
notes: When two identical vowels appear together in a Luganda word (called a long vowel), they extend the sound AND change the meaning of the word entirely. This is a very important rule because using the wrong vowel length can produce a completely different word.

luganda: Vowels Together in a Word Change Sound
english: When two vowels appear together in a Luganda word, they extend the pronunciation and sometimes give the word a different meaning. This is similar to how English vowel combinations create new sounds (e.g., 'ai', 'ou', 'ie').
notes: When two vowels appear together in a Luganda word, they extend the pronunciation and sometimes give the word a different meaning. This is similar to how English vowel combinations create new sounds (e.g., 'ai', 'ou', 'ie').

luganda: The Special Vowel: I pronounced as Yi/Ye
english: The vowel 'I' in Luganda is pronounced as 'yi' or 'ye'. This is different from English where 'i' can have multiple sounds. Always pronounce Luganda 'i' as 'yi/ye' when reading.
notes: The vowel 'I' in Luganda is pronounced as 'yi' or 'ye'. This is different from English where 'i' can have multiple sounds. Always pronounce Luganda 'i' as 'yi/ye' when reading.

luganda: The Special Vowel: U pronounced as Wu
english: The vowel 'U' in Luganda is pronounced as 'wu'. When you see a word starting with 'U' or containing 'u', pronounce it with a 'wu' sound.
notes: The vowel 'U' in Luganda is pronounced as 'wu'. When you see a word starting with 'U' or containing 'u', pronounce it with a 'wu' sound.

luganda: Words Without Vowel Endings Are Rare in Luganda
english: Unlike English, Luganda words almost never end with a consonant. English words like 'food', 'water', 'hill' all end in consonants. In Luganda, nearly every word ends in a vowel. This is an important structural feature of the language.
